title: Streaming Long‐Read Sequence Alignments for HLA Predictions Using HLAminer
author: Warren, Birol
materials: Server or machine running a 64‐bit Linux or Mac operating system with sufficient RAM (up to 35 GB)
Long sequencing reads in compressed or uncompressed FASTQ format
Reference genome for HLA sequence data

The HLAminer protocol requires a 64‐bit Linux or Mac operating system with sufficient random‐access memory (RAM) to process large volumes of DNA sequencing data (e.g., up to 35 GB RAM in our tests; see below). RAM requirements will depend on the properties of the data, including the sequencing read coverage, and the alignment parameters used. Both runtime and peak memory usage are determined by the sequence aligner used.

This protocol uses HLAminer (v1.4, https://github.com/bcgsc/hlaminer; Warren et al., 2012), a command‐line script that requires the PERL interpreter—typically pre‐installed on most Linux and Mac systems—and the minimap2 read‐aligner (2.28‐r1209, https://github.com/lh3/minimap2; Li, 2018). We recommend manually cloning and compiling the HLAminer source code from GitHub and installing minimap2 using the conda package manager.

This protocol was tested with minimap2 (Li, 2018), as it is best in class for ONT and PacBio long‐read alignments at the time of this writing, but HLAminer will support any aligners capable of outputting a SAM (Sequence Alignment/Map)‐compatible output (i.e., .sam file) with MD tags (i.e., string encoding mismatched and deleted reference bases).

Server or machine running a 64‐bit Linux or Mac operating system with sufficient RAM (up to 35 GB); we benchmarked our protocol on a dedicated server‐class CentOS Linux release 7.6.1810 system with 144 core Intel Xeon Gold 6150 CPUs at 2.70 GHz with 2.1 TB RAM.

steps.title: Confirm hardware requirements
steps.instruction: Ensure the computer runs a 64‑bit Linux or macOS OS and has sufficient RAM (up to 35 GB RAM was used in testing). For benchmarking, a server with CentOS 7.6.1810, 144 core Intel Xeon Gold 6150 CPUs at 2.70 GHz and 2.1 TB RAM was used.

steps.title: Install Miniconda and create environment
steps.instruction: Download Miniconda from https://docs.conda.io/en/latest/miniconda.html, install it, then create and activate a dedicated conda environment for the protocol.

steps.title: Install minimap2 in the environment
steps.instruction: With the “hlaminer” environment active, install minimap2 from the bioconda channel.

steps.title: Clone HLAminer repository
steps.instruction: Obtain the HLAminer source code by cloning its GitHub repository.

steps.title: Configure PATH and database variables
steps.instruction: Make HLAminer executables globally accessible and point to the reference database.

substeps.instruction: Alternatively, from the installation directory: export PATH=$(pwd)/HLAminer/HLAminer-1.4/bin:$PATH

substeps.instruction: Datasets D and E (additional ONT runs) use the same commands as dataset A

steps.title: Prepare HLA reference genome
steps.instruction: Create a reference that contains the human genome (chr‑only, no Chr6) plus all HLA genomic loci. Four alternative methods are provided; choose one.

substeps.instruction: 2. cat A_gen.fasta B_gen.fasta C_gen.fasta F_gen.fasta G_gen.fasta H_gen.fasta DP*_gen.fasta DQ*_gen.fasta DR*_gen.fasta | perl -ne 'chomp;if(/>(\S+)\s+(\S+)/){print ">>$1\n";}else{print "$_\n";}' > HLA-I_II_GEN.fasta
Option 4 – Download all reference files from Zenodo (Jan 27 2025):
If pigz or wget are unavailable, replace them with gzip or curl respectively.

steps.title: Verify reference genome file
steps.instruction: Confirm that the file GCA_000001405.15_GRCh38_genomic.chr-only-noChr6-HLA-I_II_GEN.fa.gz exists in /path/to/hlaminer/installation/HLAminer/HLAminer-1.4/database, is non‑empty and not corrupted.

steps.title: Run streaming alignment with minimap2 and HLAminer
steps.instruction: Execute minimap2 on the long‑read FASTQ (compressed or uncompressed) using the –MD flag so that MD tags are written, and pipe the SAM output directly into HLAminer in stream mode (‑a). The MD tag is required; otherwise HLAminer will produce empty output. Low coverage (<10×) may require lowering HLAminer’s minimum score threshold (‑s).

substeps.instruction: minimap2 [appropriate parameters, e.g., -ax map-ont --MD] reference.fa reads.fastq.gz | HLAminer.pl -a [additional HLAminer options]

steps.title: Review HLAminer output files
steps.instruction: Inspect the generated .csv file for allele predictions (ranked #1 and #2 per gene) and the .log file for processing details (command line, alignment statistics, scores, expect values, confidence). The .csv contains columns: Allele, Score, Expect (Eval) value, Confidence (‑10 * log10(Eval)).

steps.title: Optional: record benchmark performance
steps.instruction: Note that runtime and peak memory scale with read count; minimap2 is the primary bottleneck. In the authors’ tests, runtimes varied per dataset and correlated with the number of reads (see Table 2 of the original article).
